summary:
H.E.A.L. (Health Evaluation for Astronauts in Long term missions) is an integrated health-monitoring system designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. Its main objective is to monitor changes in the immune system and identify viral markers associated with viruses such as HSV-1, HSV-2, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), and varicella-zoster virus (VZV).

The system combines a blood sample collection device, an analytical cartridge containing specific reagents, an automated reading machine, and dedicated software. Each astronaut has a personalized identification card with a QR code linked to their information and mission ID. After the sample is analyzed, the results are stored in a digital database, allowing astronauts and medical teams on Earth to review health records and monitor changes over time.

The software prototype is being developed using Lovable, a no-code platform. H.E.A.L. aims to improve medical monitoring in space by integrating sample analysis, digital identification, automation, and data management into a compact system.
details:
What problem are we solving?

Long-duration space missions expose astronauts to several environmental and physiological stressors, including space radiation, microgravity, isolation, confinement, and sleep disturbances. These conditions can affect immune system regulation and potentially contribute to the reactivation of latent viruses.

Some viruses of interest include:

  • Herpes Simplex Virus Type 1 (HSV-1).
  • Herpes Simplex Virus Type 2 (HSV-2).
  • Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV).
  • Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV).

These viruses can remain dormant in the human body. Changes in immune function may be associated with their reactivation.

However, astronauts need reliable ways to monitor these changes during their missions, especially when access to conventional medical laboratories is limited.

H.E.A.L. addresses this challenge by proposing an integrated system for collecting biological samples, analyzing selected viral markers, and organizing health information over time.

What does H.E.A.L. do and how does it work?

H.E.A.L. consists of six main components that work together to collect, analyze, and organize astronauts' health information.

Blood Sample Collector

A small collection device is designed to obtain a superficial blood sample and retain it inside a collection capsule. The capsule is intended to contain an anticoagulant to help prevent blood clotting before analysis.

Its purpose is to make sample collection more practical and reduce the amount of equipment required.

Analytical Cartridge

The analytical cartridge receives the collected blood sample and contains the reagents required for the selected viral-marker analysis.

The proposed viral markers include:

  • HSV-1: gG1.
  • HSV-2: gG2.
  • EBV: VCA, EBNA-1, and EA-D.
  • VZV: gE and gB.

Additional reagents associated with the proposed ELISA-based detection system include:

  • HRP (Horseradish Peroxidase): An enzyme used to generate a detectable signal.
  • TMB (Tetramethylbenzidine): A substrate that produces a color change in the presence of HRP.
  • Wash Solution: Used to remove unbound substances during the analytical process.

These components are associated with immunological detection. The final cartridge design must be validated to establish which antibodies or antigens are being measured.

Astronaut Identification Card

Each astronaut has an individual identification card containing a QR code.

The QR code links to three identification details:

  • Astronaut's name.
  • Astronaut identification number.
  • Blood type.

The card is designed to be reusable and properly disinfected after each analysis.

Before processing a sample, the machine scans the QR code to identify the astronaut and associate the analysis with the correct digital health record.

This helps prevent results from being assigned to the wrong astronaut.

Automated Analysis Machine

The machine is the main hardware component of H.E.A.L.

Its proposed operation follows three main stages:

  • It scans the astronaut's identification card and retrieves the corresponding profile.
  • It receives the analytical cartridge containing the biological sample and selected reagents.
  • It processes the cartridge and obtains the analytical results for digital registration.

The machine is intended to automate the analysis and reduce the need for astronauts to perform complex laboratory procedures themselves.

The specific reader technology, detection mechanism, and hardware specifications remain part of the engineering development and validation process.

H.E.A.L. Software

The software is responsible for receiving, organizing, displaying, and storing the analytical results.

The prototype is being developed using Lovable, a no-code development platform that allows users to create software interfaces and functional demonstrations without requiring advanced programming knowledge.

The proposed software features include:

  • Astronaut identification and individual profiles.
  • QR-code identification.
  • Registration of biological sample analyses.
  • Display of detected viral markers.
  • Historical records of previous analyses.
  • Comparison of results over time.
  • A centralized database accessible from the spacecraft and the ground-based medical team.

The software is intended to transform individual test results into organized health records that can support medical assessment and decision-making.

Ground-Based Database

H.E.A.L. also proposes connecting the onboard system with a database on Earth.

This would allow medical personnel to access information transmitted from space, review historical records, and study changes in astronauts' health throughout their missions.

The system could contribute to research on immune-system changes and viral activity during long-duration spaceflight.

What benefits does H.E.A.L. offer?

H.E.A.L. offers several potential benefits:

  • Health monitoring: Helps organize repeated analyses and track changes in selected viral markers.
  • Early identification of concerning results: Can alert medical personnel when results require further evaluation.
  • Improved medical support: Provides astronauts and medical teams with organized health information.
  • Digital identification: Associates each analysis with the correct astronaut.
  • Automated data management: Reduces manual recordkeeping and facilitates access to historical information.
  • Scientific research: Can contribute to collecting long-term data about viral markers and immune-system responses during space missions.

It is important to distinguish between detecting viral antibodies and detecting active viral replication. An antibody-based ELISA result alone cannot confirm that a latent virus has reactivated. Additional molecular testing, such as PCR, may be necessary to investigate viral activity.

What is the expected impact of the project?

H.E.A.L. aims to generate medical, scientific, technological, operational, and human impact.

Medical Impact: Provides additional information that can support the evaluation of astronauts' immune health.

Scientific Impact: Contributes to research on viral markers, immune-system changes, and the physiological effects of long-duration spaceflight.

Technological Impact: Integrates biological sample analysis, digital identification, automation, and software into one proposed system.

Operational Impact: Could reduce dependence on Earth-based laboratory testing for selected analyses and improve access to health information aboard spacecraft.

Human Impact: Supports astronaut well-being by helping medical personnel identify changes that require attention and make more informed decisions.

What makes H.E.A.L. creative and innovative?

H.E.A.L. is creative because it proposes adapting existing biomedical technologies to the specific challenges of space exploration.

Rather than relying on a single diagnostic test, the project integrates sample collection, analytical cartridges, digital identification, automated reading, and health-data management.

Its innovation lies in combining these elements into a compact system designed for environments where medical resources, available space, and access to Earth-based laboratories are limited.

The system also considers the possibility of expanding its analytical capabilities to monitor additional health indicators in the future.

What factors did our team consider?

During the development of H.E.A.L., our team considered several important factors:

  • Practicality: The device should be compact and occupy as little space as possible.
  • Ease of Use: Astronauts should be able to operate the system without complicated laboratory procedures.
  • Analytical Reliability: The system should provide consistent and scientifically valid results.
  • Automation: The process should require minimal manual intervention.
  • Identification and Data Organization: Each result must be associated with the correct astronaut.
  • Space Environment Compatibility: Components and reagents must be evaluated for stability under microgravity, radiation, temperature variations, and vibration.
  • Long-Term Usability: The system should be adaptable to different mission durations and future analytical requirements.

What tools, programming languages, hardware, and software are used?

Software Development

  • Lovable: A no-code platform used to develop the software prototype and simulate the system's interface and functions.

Proposed Hardware

  • Blood sample collection device.
  • Analytical cartridge.
  • Reusable QR-code identification card.
  • Automated cartridge-reading machine.
  • Data storage and communication components.

Proposed Analytical Technology

  • ELISA-related immunological detection components.
  • HRP enzyme.
  • TMB substrate.
  • Wash solution.
  • Selected viral antigens or antibodies, depending on the final assay design.

No specific programming language or microcontroller has been confirmed as part of the current prototype. The software is currently a no-code demonstration rather than a fully integrated medical diagnostic system.

What are our future plans?

Our team plans to continue improving H.E.A.L. through several development goals.

Improve the Device's Practicality

Make the system more compact, easier to operate, and better adapted to the conditions of space missions.

Expand Viral Detection Capabilities

Include additional viral targets and investigate more comprehensive analytical panels to monitor different aspects of astronauts' immune health.

Integrate Additional Health Indicators

Explore the possibility of incorporating glucose detection and other health-monitoring functions to expand the system beyond viral analysis.

Develop More Advanced Software

Improve the software's ability to organize results, compare historical records, display health trends, and facilitate communication between astronauts and medical personnel on Earth.

Adapt H.E.A.L. to Other Extreme Environments

Explore applications in submarines, isolated research facilities, and other environments where access to conventional medical laboratories is limited.

Prepare the System for Future Planetary Exploration

Investigate how H.E.A.L. could be adapted for future missions to Mars, where astronauts will need greater medical independence and reliable onboard health-monitoring technologies.

How does H.E.A.L. relate to the mission?

The mission challenges teams to develop health-monitoring software that collects health indicators and allows astronauts to evaluate their condition and take appropriate action.

H.E.A.L. directly addresses this objective by proposing a system that connects biological sample analysis with digital health monitoring.

It allows the proposed analytical device to generate information that can be stored, reviewed, and compared over time through dedicated software.

Therefore, H.E.A.L. supports the mission's goal of increasing astronauts' ability to monitor their own health during long-duration space missions while providing medical teams on Earth with additional information to support their assessments.

How can H.E.A.L. differentiate itself from other products on the market?

H.E.A.L. aims to differentiate itself through the integration of several functions into one proposed platform:

  • Biological sample collection and analysis.
  • Individual QR-code identification.
  • Automated result registration.
  • Historical health records.
  • Communication between onboard systems and Earth-based medical teams.
  • Potential expansion to additional health indicators.

Its main differentiating feature is not the invention of a completely new diagnostic technology, but the adaptation and integration of existing technologies into a system specifically designed for the operational challenges of long-duration space missions.

This approach could make H.E.A.L. a versatile health-monitoring platform for astronauts and potentially other isolated environments in the future.
